C005.subject: A policy that succeeds only when it fails under its stated metric
C005.object: a shift from outcome-based to resilience-based evaluation, where success is measured by the system's capacity to absorb disruption and maintain function after the policy's intended targets are missed
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: A policy that succeeds only when it fails under its stated metric a shift from outcome-based to resilience-based evaluation, where success is measured by the system's capacity to absorb disruption and maintain function after the policy's intended targets are missed]

[PATH:empirical] Case study analysis of 'fail-forward' policies in disaster management (e.g., FEMA's National Flood Insurance Program reforms) where stated loss-reduction targets were missed but community resilience improved — Directly tests the hypothesis by examining real-world policies that failed under their own metrics yet enhanced system absorption capacity, providing evidence for or against the required shift to resilience-based evaluation.

[PATH:theoretical] Formal modeling of adaptive policy cycles (e.g., Holling's panarchy theory applied to regulatory systems) comparing outcome-based vs. resilience-based evaluation metrics in simulated policy environments — Enables controlled testing of the logical necessity of the shift, clarifying whether resilience-based evaluation is a requirement or merely a correlate when policies fail under stated metrics.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review of policy evaluation frameworks in complex adaptive systems literature (e.g., articles in 'Ecology and Society' or 'Policy Sciences' on resilience metrics) — Surveys existing theoretical and empirical work to identify whether the hypothesized causal relationship is supported, refuted, or underdetermined by current knowledge.

C006.subject: A policy that succeeds only when it fails under its stated metric

evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: A policy that succeeds only when it fails under its stated metric in organizations where metric selection is decoupled from stakeholder feedback loops, because the disconnect prevents correction of misaligned indicators]

[PATH:empirical] Case studies of metric-driven policy failures in public sector organizations (e.g., UK's 'targets and terror' in healthcare or US No Child Left Behind), analyzing whether stakeholder feedback was integrated into metric design — Directly tests the hypothesis by examining real-world instances where policies succeeded under official metrics but failed in practice, and whether these cases exhibited decoupled stakeholder feedback loops

[PATH:literature] Organizational behavior literature on 'metric fixation' and 'gaming the system' (e.g., Jerry Z. Muller's 'The Tyranny of Metrics'), with a focus on how feedback loop decoupling perpetuates misaligned indicators — Provides theoretical grounding and documented patterns that support or challenge the causal mechanism of stakeholder feedback decoupling leading to perverse metric-driven outcomes

[PATH:empirical] Controlled experiments or agent-based modeling comparing policy outcomes under coupled vs. decoupled metric-feedback conditions in simulated organizational contexts — Allows isolation of the decoupling variable to establish causal direction, controlling for confounds like organizational culture or external pressures

scope.domain: organizational policy design and metric governance

qualifier.geographic: primarily Western and industrialized economies with formal metric governance structures

C007.subject: The same policy pattern
C007.object: regimes facing imminent electoral loss or internal legitimacy crises, as a last-resort tool to consolidate power by deliberately sabotaging the public metric to trigger a manufactured crisis
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: The same policy pattern regimes facing imminent electoral loss or internal legitimacy crises, as a last-resort tool to consolidate power by deliberately sabotaging the public metric to trigger a manufactured crisis]

[PATH:empirical] Comparative case studies of electoral authoritarian regimes (e.g., Hungary 2010-2014, Venezuela 2013, Turkey 2017) that manipulated economic indicators or public service metrics prior to contested elections, using process tracing to identify intent and timing. — Directly tests whether the pattern of deliberately sabotaging public metrics occurs specifically as a last-resort tool before imminent electoral loss, by examining documented instances of metric manipulation and subsequent manufactured crises.

[PATH:theoretical] Formal game-theoretic models of regime crisis behavior, e.g., models of 'manufactured crises' or 'diversionary theory' applied to hybrid regimes, such as those by Bueno de Mesquita or Svolik, extended to include strategic metric sabotage. — Provides a deductive framework to predict when and why regimes would choose to sabotage public metrics, helping to distinguish this hypothesis from alternative explanations like incompetence or genuine policy failure.

[PATH:empirical] Large-N statistical analysis of cross-national data on election outcomes, legitimacy indicators (e.g., protest events, executive approval), and public metric integrity (e.g., inflation reporting, unemployment data) from 1990-2024, using datasets like V-Dem or Polity. — Enables quantitative testing of whether metric sabotage correlates with imminent electoral loss or legitimacy crises, controlling for other factors, and can reveal whether the pattern is exclusive to such regimes or more widespread.

qualifier.temporal: during periods of regime instability or contested elections, 1990–2024
qualifier.geographic: in hybrid regimes and backsliding democracies with fragmented bureaucracies
